content.comment_body: Hello, I have a challenge. I need to control two digital inputs and one digital output. DI1 is triggered by an alarm—its contact stays closed while the alarm is active. DI2 acts as a push button to stop the process, and DO1 sends signals to another system. When DI1 activates, DO1 should immediately receive one pulse. If after 30 seconds DI2 stays at 0, DO1 receives two pulses; if this remains for another 30 seconds, DO1 receives three pulses. This loops, and upon toggling DI2 (press and release), the pulses and loop stop. DI1 can then be reset manually to restart the process. I've tried various configurations with pulse relays and delayed switches, but nothing seems to work well. Does anyone have suggestions?

I recommend using several timers, such as ON-Delays and edge-triggered wiping relays, where you can specify the number of pulse cycles. For example, you can trigger a wiping relay with one pulse after 30 seconds, another with two pulses after 60 seconds, and so forth. Alternatively, up/down counters could also work for this task. Regards, [user_name]

Thanks for your input. My initial mistake was chaining ON delays one after another, which led to confusion in the process. I reworked the setup and used edge-triggered wiping relays alongside regular wiping relays, and now everything functions correctly.

Just a reminder: the timer logic you've implemented may behave differently on actual [product_name] hardware compared to simulation on a PC. Timing functions, especially those that depend on each other, can act unpredictably due to the way the Java environment simulates them on different computers. From experience, it's important to validate your code on physical hardware. Cheers!
You're right, I've noticed the difference myself. For my situation, though, a discrepancy of a couple of seconds isn't critical.

analysis.insight_summary: Users worked to design a pulse sequence for a digital output using timers and relays on [company_name] programmable devices. Major challenges occurred when ON delays were chained incorrectly, causing erratic behavior. Discussions revealed that timing logic behaves differently in software simulation versus real hardware because of the way Java executes timers on PCs, leading to inconsistent results. Users acknowledged the importance of testing timer-dependent logic directly on hardware for reliable operation.
analysis.user_expectations: Users are looking for straightforward, reliable timer and relay logic setups that make pulse generation consistent across simulation and actual hardware, minimizing the need for extensive troubleshooting during implementation.
